*Pre-Assignment*
Load all necessary packages, read in the clinical data.csv file you have in your analysis_data folder, and instantiate the MAF_object.
```{r}

# Partner name(s) here, if any

knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath("~/490_cluster/analysis_data"))
                     
library(BiocManager)
library(TCGAbiolinks)
library(maftools)
library(readr)

setwd("~/490_cluster/analysis_data")
clinical <- read_csv("brca_clinical_data.csv")

maf_query <- GDCquery(
project = "TCGA-BRCA",
data.category = "Simple Nucleotide Variation",
access = "open",
data.type = "Masked Somatic Mutation",
workflow.type = "Aliquot Ensemble Somatic Variant Merging and Masking"
)

GDCdownload(maf_query)

maf_prepared <- GDCprepare(maf_query)

clinical$Tumor_Sample_Barcode <- clinical$patient_id

maf_object <- read.maf(
  maf = maf_prepared,
  clinicalData = clinical,
  isTCGA = TRUE
)

```

It's useful to save your MAF_object, so that you don't have to go through the trouble of querying and preparing it everytime. The saveRDS function allows us to save an R object, allowing us to access it directly from our files. 
```{r}
saveRDS(maf_object, file = "~/490_cluster/analysis_data/maf_object.rds")
# ex. saveRDS(MAF_object, file = "/home1/yourname/490_cluster/analysis_data/maf_object.rds")
```

When you reopen a new R session and want to access your MAF_object, you can use the readRDS function to load the object back into a new variable.
```{r}

er <- maf_object@clinical.data$er_status_by_ihc
er[!er %in% c("Positive", "Negative")] <- NA

maf_object@clinical.data$er_factor <- factor(er, levels = c("Positive", "Negative"))

table(maf_object@clinical.data$er_factor, useNA = "ifany")

pos_mask <- !is.na(maf_object@clinical.data$er_factor) & maf_object@clinical.data$er_factor == "Positive"
neg_mask <- !is.na(maf_object@clinical.data$er_factor) & maf_object@clinical.data$er_factor == "Negative"

pos_barcodes <- maf_object@clinical.data$Tumor_Sample_Barcode[pos_mask]
neg_barcodes <- maf_object@clinical.data$Tumor_Sample_Barcode[neg_mask]

pos_object <- subsetMaf(maf = maf_object, tsb = pos_barcodes)
neg_object <- subsetMaf(maf = maf_object, tsb = neg_barcodes)

```


*2*
Create a co-oncoplot with the top 10-20 (you choose) most mutated genes for the two groups. Pick one that has a large discrepancy in % mutated or type of mutations between the groups and research it. 
Research it. What is the gene used for? Can you think of any reason for the discrepancy?
```{r}

top_pos <- getGeneSummary(pos_object)$Hugo_Symbol[1:10]
top_neg <- getGeneSummary(neg_object)$Hugo_Symbol[1:10]
genes_to_plot <- unique(c(top_pos, top_neg))
genes_to_plot

png("er_status_coOncoplot_top_genes.png", width = 1200, height = 900)
coOncoplot(m1 = pos_object,
           m2 = neg_object,
           genes = genes_to_plot,
           m1Name = "ER Positive",
           m2Name = "ER Negative")
dev.off()

coOncoplot(m1 = pos_object,
           m2 = neg_object,
           genes = genes_to_plot,
           m1Name = "ER Positive",
           m2Name = "ER Negative")

pos_summary <- getGeneSummary(pos_object)
neg_summary <- getGeneSummary(neg_object)
n_pos <- nrow(pos_object@clinical.data)
n_neg <- nrow(neg_object@clinical.data)

get_pct <- function(summary_df, gene, n) {
  x <- summary_df$MutatedSamples[summary_df$Hugo_Symbol == gene]
  if (length(x) == 0) 0 else x / n * 100
}

comp <- data.frame(
  Gene = genes_to_plot,
  pct_ER_pos = sapply(genes_to_plot, get_pct, summary_df = pos_summary, n = n_pos),
  pct_ER_neg = sapply(genes_to_plot, get_pct, summary_df = neg_summary, n = n_neg)
)
comp$diff <- comp$pct_ER_pos - comp$pct_ER_neg
comp[order(-abs(comp$diff)), ]

#TP53 is mutated 81% of the time in ER neg tumors but only 21% of time time in ER pos tumors. TP53 is responsible for encoding p53, the tumor suppresor gene. ER neg tumors are more aggresive so it makes sense that there would be more mutated p53

```


*3*
Create a contingency table with your variable and chosen gene. Run a Fisher’s Exact Test between presence of mutations for that gene and your clinical variable. Create and save a mosaic plot. 
Interpret the output of the Fisher’s Exact Test in terms of the odds ratio and p-value.
```{r}

TP53_maf <- subsetMaf(maf = maf_object, genes = "TP53")

mutation_status <- ifelse(maf_object@clinical.data$Tumor_Sample_Barcode %in%
                            TP53_maf@clinical.data$Tumor_Sample_Barcode,
                          "mutation", "no_mutation")

contingency_table <- table(mutation_status, maf_object@clinical.data$er_factor)
contingency_table

fisher_result <- fisher.test(contingency_table)
fisher_result

png("TP53_vs_ER_status_mosaic_plot.png", width = 800, height = 600)
mosaicplot(contingency_table,
           main = "TP53 Mutation Status by ER Status",
           xlab = "TP53 Mutation Status",
           ylab = "ER Status",
           color = TRUE)
dev.off()

mosaicplot(contingency_table,
           main = "TP53 Mutation Status by ER Status",
           xlab = "TP53 Mutation Status",
           ylab = "ER Status",
           color = TRUE)

#The odds ratio of 0.061 means that there is a 16.5x (1/0.061) chance that TP53 is mutated in ER neg tumors than ER pos. The P value is far below 0.05, so we can reject the null hypothesis that TP53 mutation odds and ER status are independent.
```

*5*
Create your Overall_Survival_Status column and create a mafSurvival KM plot based on mutations in your chosen gene.
Does there seem to be a difference? Hypothesize why or not based on the other analysis you did with the gene above.
```{r}

vs <- maf_object@clinical.data$vital_status

maf_object@clinical.data$Overall_Survival_Status <- ifelse(vs == "Dead", TRUE,
                                                    ifelse(vs == "Alive", FALSE, NA))

maf_object@clinical.data$survival_time <- ifelse(vs == "Dead",
  suppressWarnings(as.numeric(maf_object@clinical.data$death_days_to)),
  suppressWarnings(as.numeric(maf_object@clinical.data$last_contact_days_to)))

table(maf_object@clinical.data$Overall_Survival_Status, useNA = "ifany")
summary(maf_object@clinical.data$survival_time)

png("TP53_mafSurvival_KM_plot.png", width = 800, height = 600)
mafSurvival(maf = maf_object,
            genes = "TP53",
            time = "survival_time",
            Status = "Overall_Survival_Status",
            isTCGA = TRUE)
dev.off()

mafSurvival(maf = maf_object,
            genes = "TP53",
            time = "survival_time",
            Status = "Overall_Survival_Status",
            isTCGA = TRUE)

#HR of 1.42 means that mutant patients have a 42% higher chance of death than WT patients. However, the P value is greater than 0.05 so the results are not statistically significant. After about 4000 days, the lines flatten, probalby meaning that there are few patients left in the study. Without p53, cells are less regulated than WT patients, resulting in the earlier drop in survival rate on the graph for mutant patients.

```
